summary: This migration replaces the entire container lifecycle infrastructure (~4,000+ lines of Docker code) with Kubernetes equivalents. The change is high-risk due to: (1) security-critical network isolation that must be faithfully replicated, (2) complex storage/worktree patterns that rely on Docker-specific primitives, (3) no rollback path after merge (Option A full cutover), and (4) broad blast radius across CI, CLI, tests, and deployment. The risks are manageable with proper phasing, but several areas require human review before implementation begins.

risks.title: Network isolation regression — agent sandbox escape
risks.description: The current Docker network model enforces fail-closed isolation: the `egg-isolated` network uses Docker's `internal: true` flag, physically preventing containers from reaching the internet. DNS is locked to 0.0.0.0 for private-mode agents. All traffic must route through gateway's Squid proxy. The k8s replacement uses Calico NetworkPolicies, which are a software-level enforcement mechanism — misconfigurations silently fail open. A single missing or misconfigured NetworkPolicy could allow agent pods to bypass the gateway and reach the internet directly, breaking the entire security model.
mitigation: Implement default-deny ingress AND egress NetworkPolicies in egg-agents namespace before deploying any agent pods
Add explicit egress whitelist: agents can ONLY reach the gateway Service on specific ports (9848, 3129)
Port the full integration_tests/test_network_isolation.py suite to k8s — these tests MUST pass before merge
Add a 'canary' integration test that spawns an agent pod and verifies it CANNOT reach an external endpoint (e.g., httpbin.org)
Document the NetworkPolicy manifests with comments explaining the security model they enforce
Consider adding a Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy as a backstop that denies all egress from the egg-agents namespace to any IP outside the cluster
risks.rollback_plan: If network isolation is broken post-deploy, immediately delete all agent Jobs in egg-agents namespace (`kubectl delete jobs -n egg-agents --all`). Apply emergency default-deny NetworkPolicy. No data is at risk — agents only have access to repo worktrees.
risks.human_review_reason: Security-critical change. The network isolation model is the primary defense against agent sandbox escape. A security engineer should review the NetworkPolicy manifests and validate they enforce equivalent isolation to the Docker model.

risks.title: Calico CNI installation and compatibility with k3s
risks.description: k3s ships with Flannel as default CNI, which does NOT support NetworkPolicies. The migration requires installing k3s with `--flannel-backend=none --disable-network-policy` and then installing Calico separately. This is a well-documented but non-trivial setup. Known issues include: (1) dual-stack IPv6 DNS resolution failures with Calico on k3s (k3s-io/k3s#5743), (2) cross-node service access issues after applying NetworkPolicies in multi-node clusters (projectcalico/calico#4919), (3) Calico must be installed before any pods are scheduled — ordering matters. Additionally, Calico adds operational complexity (Felix agent, BIRD BGP daemon, etcd or KDD datastore).
mitigation: Pin Calico to a specific tested version (e.g., v3.27.x) — do not use 'latest'
Create an automated `make k3s-setup` target that handles the full sequence: k3s install with correct flags, Calico apply, readiness wait
Add a smoke test that verifies NetworkPolicies are enforced before proceeding (`kubectl apply` a test deny-all policy, verify a test pod cannot egress)
Document the exact k3s + Calico versions tested and any known incompatibilities
Consider Cilium as an alternative CNI — it also supports NetworkPolicies and has better eBPF-based enforcement, but adds more complexity
risks.rollback_plan: If Calico fails to install or causes networking issues, the entire k3s cluster can be destroyed and recreated (`k3s-uninstall.sh`). This is a local-only deployment, so blast radius is limited to the developer's machine.

risks.title: Shared filesystem / worktree isolation breaks in k8s
risks.description: The current architecture relies heavily on Docker bind mounts for worktree isolation. Gateway manages worktrees at `/home/egg/.egg-worktrees/<container_id>/<repo_name>` on the host, and agent containers mount them directly. In k8s, this requires shared filesystem access between gateway pods and agent pods. The k3s local-path-provisioner only supports ReadWriteOnce (RWO) by default — NOT ReadWriteMany (RWX). Worktree sharing requires either: hostPath volumes (not portable), NFS provisioner (added complexity), or the local-path-provisioner's `sharedFileSystemPath` option (non-standard). Additionally, the per-agent worktree lifecycle (create on spawn, detect uncommitted changes on exit, cleanup) must be replicated with k8s primitives.
mitigation: For local k3s (single-node): use hostPath volumes initially — both gateway and agent pods see the same host filesystem. This matches current Docker behavior.
Define a clear `StorageBackend` interface so the hostPath implementation can be swapped for NFS/Longhorn when moving to multi-node GKE
Replicate phase-based readonly enforcement using k8s volume mount `readOnly: true` on specific subpaths
Implement worktree lifecycle as a sidecar or init container pattern: init container requests worktree from gateway API, main container uses it, cleanup sidecar handles post-exit detection
Add integration tests that verify: (a) agent pod can read/write its worktree, (b) agent pod CANNOT access another agent's worktree, (c) readonly phase mounts are enforced
risks.rollback_plan: Worktree isolation is per-pipeline. If broken, affected pipelines can be re-run. No persistent data loss — worktrees are ephemeral copies of git branches.
risks.human_review_reason: The worktree sharing model is architecturally significant. The chosen approach (hostPath vs NFS vs API-based) has long-term implications for multi-node scalability. Decision 2 from the analysis should be resolved before implementation.

risks.title: .git shadow mount pattern not directly portable to k8s
risks.description: The current sandbox uses a .git shadow mount (tmpfs overlay or /dev/null bind mount on the .git directory/file) to force all git operations through the gateway API. This prevents agents from running native git commands that bypass policy enforcement. In Docker, this is done with `tmpfs` mounts on specific paths inside the container. Kubernetes doesn't natively support overlaying tmpfs on arbitrary paths within a volume — it uses volume mounts at the pod level. The .git file (gitdir link in worktrees) is shadowed with a /dev/null bind mount (container_spawner.py), which requires `hostPath` type `CharDevice` or a custom init container.
mitigation: Use an init container that prepares the worktree filesystem: copy worktree contents into an emptyDir volume, replace .git with a non-functional stub, then start the main container with the prepared volume
Alternatively, mount the .git path as an emptyDir volume (which overlays the parent volume at that path), effectively hiding the real .git
Test that `git status`, `git push`, `git commit` all fail or route through gateway wrapper scripts when the shadow mount is active
Document the shadow mount k8s implementation clearly — this is a non-obvious security mechanism
risks.rollback_plan: If shadow mount fails, agents gain direct git access but the gateway wrapper scripts still intercept common git commands. This is a defense-in-depth layer, not the sole control.

risks.title: IP-based gateway session binding removal weakens auth model
risks.description: The current gateway binds each session token to a specific container IP address (session_manager.py lines 273-310, 649-656). This provides defense-in-depth: even if a session token leaks, it can only be used from the specific container it was issued to. The migration proposes removing IP-based binding since pod IPs are ephemeral in k8s. Moving to token-only auth means a leaked token can be used from ANY pod. The session token is passed via environment variable (EGG_SESSION_TOKEN), which is visible in k8s pod specs and potentially in logs.
affected_files: gateway/session_manager.py (lines 273-310, session creation with IP binding)
sandbox/egg_lib/runtime.py (lines 178-269, IP allocation and session setup)
mitigation: Use Kubernetes Secrets (not env vars) for session tokens — prevents exposure in pod specs and `kubectl describe pod` output
Implement short-lived tokens with automatic rotation (e.g., 1-hour TTL with refresh)
Add pod identity binding: bind session tokens to the pod's ServiceAccount token or UID instead of IP. The k8s downward API can inject pod UID.
Implement session scoping: each token should only permit operations on the specific pipeline/repo/branch assigned to that agent
Add audit logging for all gateway API calls with the session token, source pod identity, and operation performed
Consider mutual TLS between agent pods and gateway for stronger authentication
risks.rollback_plan: If token-based auth is compromised, invalidate all active sessions via gateway API. Gateway already supports session invalidation on cleanup.
risks.human_review_reason: Security model change. Removing IP-based binding is a deliberate weakening of one authentication factor. A security engineer should validate the replacement mechanism provides equivalent or better protection.

risks.title: Big-bang cutover with no rollback path
risks.description: Option A (full cutover) removes ALL Docker code simultaneously. Once merged, there is no rollback to the Docker-based system. If critical issues are discovered post-merge (e.g., k3s doesn't work on a team member's machine, Calico causes networking issues, k8s Jobs have unexpected behavior differences from Docker containers), the team is stuck with a broken system until fixes land. The changeset is estimated at 4,000+ lines of code replaced, affecting 6+ core modules.
mitigation: Even though Option A was selected, implement the `ContainerBackend` protocol (as noted in the issue) and keep the Docker implementation in a `_deprecated/` directory or separate branch for 2-4 weeks post-merge
Create a comprehensive acceptance test suite that validates the full pipeline lifecycle (spawn → execute → monitor → cleanup) on k8s BEFORE removing Docker code
Merge in phases via stacked PRs: (1) add k8s code + ContainerBackend protocol, (2) switch default to k8s, (3) remove Docker code — this gives escape hatches between each phase
Ensure `make k3s-setup` works on all team members' environments BEFORE merging the cutover
Tag the last Docker-based commit for easy revert: `git tag docker-last-v1`
risks.rollback_plan: If critical issues found immediately post-merge: `git revert` the merge commit to restore Docker code. If issues found later: `git checkout docker-last-v1` to create a hotfix branch. The stacked-PR approach (mitigation) provides cleaner rollback points.
risks.human_review_reason: Migration strategy decision. The team should confirm they are comfortable with full cutover vs. a phased approach. The stacked-PR mitigation should be discussed before implementation begins.

risks.title: CI pipeline breakage during migration
risks.description: GitHub Actions workflows (test-integration.yml, test-e2e.yml, release-images.yml) currently use `docker build` and `docker compose`. The migration requires k3s to be available in CI runners. GitHub Actions runners DO support k3s installation, but it adds ~60-90 seconds to workflow startup, changes the test execution model entirely, and introduces a new failure mode (k3s installation failures in CI). The release-images.yml workflow pushes to GHCR — this should remain Docker-based since image building and image runtime are independent concerns.
mitigation: Keep release-images.yml using Docker buildx for image building — GHCR is Docker-registry-compatible regardless of runtime
Create a reusable GitHub Actions step for k3s setup (install k3s, install Calico, wait for ready) to share across workflows
Add k3s installation caching in CI to reduce setup time
Run integration tests in a dedicated k3s namespace per workflow run to prevent cross-run interference
Add a CI-specific overlay in Kustomize: `overlays/ci/` with appropriate resource limits and timeouts for GitHub Actions runners
Keep old CI workflows on a branch until new ones are validated for at least 1 week
risks.rollback_plan: CI workflows are independently deployable via workflow_dispatch. Keep the old workflow files in a `ci-backup` branch. If new CI breaks, restore old workflows and revert the infrastructure PR.

risks.title: Container monitoring behavior changes with k8s Jobs
risks.description: The current ContainerMonitor (884 lines) uses Docker events API for real-time container state changes (STARTED/STOPPED/EXITED/FAILED/UNHEALTHY) with 10-second polling as fallback. k8s Job monitoring uses the Watch API or polling via the k8s Python client, which has different semantics: pod phase transitions (Pending→Running→Succeeded/Failed), container restart events, and OOMKilled signals. The orchestrator's concurrent_executor.py relies on specific callback patterns (spawn_fn returns container_id, monitor detects exit) that must be faithfully replicated. Subtle behavior differences (e.g., k8s Job `backoffLimit` vs Docker restart policy, pod eviction vs container OOM) could cause agent lifecycle bugs.
mitigation: Map Docker container states to k8s pod/Job states explicitly in documentation
Use k8s Watch API for real-time events (equivalent to Docker events), with polling fallback
Set `backoffLimit: 0` on all agent Jobs to prevent k8s from auto-restarting failed agents (orchestrator manages retries)
Set `activeDeadlineSeconds` to match current timeout mechanisms
Add comprehensive unit tests for the KubernetesMonitor that verify all state transition callbacks fire correctly
Test OOMKilled handling explicitly — k8s reports this differently than Docker
risks.rollback_plan: Monitor issues are observable and debuggable. The ContainerBackend protocol allows swapping implementations. Monitor bugs don't cause data loss — at worst, agents need to be re-spawned.

risks.title: Developer experience regression — k3s as new prerequisite
risks.description: The migration replaces Docker (ubiquitous, well-understood) with k3s as a prerequisite for local development. k3s is Linux-native — macOS and Windows users need a Linux VM (Lima, Rancher Desktop, or WSL2). This adds friction for developers. Additionally, Calico CNI installation, NetworkPolicy debugging, and k8s-specific troubleshooting (kubectl logs, describe pod, events) require different skillsets than Docker troubleshooting.
mitigation: Create a comprehensive `make k3s-setup` that handles the full setup automatically (k3s install, Calico, image import, readiness check)
Add a `make k3s-status` target for diagnosing common issues
Document the setup for macOS (Lima or Rancher Desktop) and Windows (WSL2) explicitly
Add a troubleshooting guide covering common k3s/Calico issues
Consider providing a `Vagrantfile` or `lima.yaml` for macOS/Windows users
risks.rollback_plan: Developer experience issues are not blocking — they can be iteratively improved post-merge.

risks.title: kubernetes Python client — new dependency with large surface area
risks.description: Adding the `kubernetes` Python client introduces a significant new dependency tree. The k8s Python client is maintained by the Kubernetes SIG and is generally well-maintained. No specific CVEs were found for the Python client in 2025-2026, though the broader k8s ecosystem has had critical vulnerabilities (e.g., Ingress NGINX CVE-2025-1974, runc CVE-2025-31133). The client requires RBAC configuration (ServiceAccount + ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding) for the orchestrator pod — over-permissioned RBAC is a common k8s security anti-pattern.
mitigation: Pin the kubernetes Python client to a specific version and add to dependency scanning (safety/bandit)
Follow least-privilege RBAC: orchestrator ServiceAccount should only have permissions for Jobs, Pods, and Logs in the egg-agents namespace — NOT cluster-admin
Deny access to Secrets, ConfigMaps, and other sensitive resources unless explicitly needed
Add RBAC manifests to code review with a comment explaining each permission
Run `safety check` against the new dependency before merging
risks.rollback_plan: Dependency can be removed if migration is reverted. RBAC roles are namespace-scoped and can be deleted with `kubectl delete`.

risks.title: File-based locking (fcntl) incompatible with k8s multi-pod model
risks.description: The current code uses `fcntl.flock()` for IP allocation locking (runtime.py lines 216-268) to prevent concurrent IP conflicts. While this is only relevant for the CLI runtime (not pipeline-spawned agents), any code that relies on file-based locking will break if multiple orchestrator replicas are running. For the initial single-node k3s deployment this is low-impact, but it creates technical debt for multi-node scaling.
mitigation: For single-node k3s (initial target): hostPath volumes preserve file-lock semantics — this works unchanged
For future multi-node: replace fcntl locks with k8s Lease objects or ConfigMap-based optimistic locking
Document the single-node assumption in the code with a TODO for multi-node migration
risks.rollback_plan: N/A — low impact for initial deployment. Address when scaling to multi-node.

risks.title: Integration test rewrite scope and coverage gap risk
risks.description: The integration test suite includes critical security tests (test_network_isolation.py — 434 lines, test_network_security.py — 95 lines) and pipeline lifecycle tests that use docker-compose and `docker exec`. These tests MUST be rewritten for k8s (`kubectl exec`, k8s Job assertions). During the rewrite, there is a risk that test coverage is reduced — either by accidentally omitting test cases or by the k8s test equivalents not testing the same security properties. The local_pipeline integration tests (docker-compose.yml — 126 lines) test the full spawn→execute→cleanup lifecycle with a mock sandbox.
mitigation: Create a test coverage checklist mapping every existing integration test to its k8s equivalent BEFORE starting the rewrite
Require that ALL existing test_network_isolation.py test cases have k8s equivalents before merging
Add new k8s-specific tests: NetworkPolicy enforcement, pod-to-pod isolation, namespace isolation
Run both old (Docker) and new (k8s) test suites in parallel during development to catch coverage gaps
Mark any test cases that cannot be ported with a TODO and justification
risks.rollback_plan: Test infrastructure is independent of production code. Old tests can be restored from git history if needed.
risks.human_review_reason: The security integration tests are critical safety nets. A reviewer should verify that the k8s test suite provides equivalent coverage to the Docker test suite, particularly for network isolation properties.

items_requiring_human_review.topic: NetworkPolicy manifests for agent sandbox isolation
items_requiring_human_review.reason: Security-critical: network isolation is the primary defense against agent sandbox escape. Misconfigured NetworkPolicies fail open, not closed.

items_requiring_human_review.topic: Shared filesystem approach for worktree isolation
items_requiring_human_review.reason: Architectural decision with long-term implications. The open question (Decision 2 in analysis) about hostPath vs NFS vs API-based worktree access must be resolved.
Removing IP-based session binding is a deliberate reduction in authentication factors. Replacement mechanism must provide equivalent protection.

items_requiring_human_review.topic: Full cutover migration strategy vs phased approach
items_requiring_human_review.reason: High-impact decision. The team should explicitly confirm comfort level with no rollback path, or agree on the stacked-PR mitigation.

items_requiring_human_review.topic: Integration test coverage parity during rewrite
items_requiring_human_review.reason: Security test coverage must not regress. Explicit sign-off that k8s tests cover all Docker test scenarios.

open_decisions_blocking_implementation.question: Should the migration use stacked PRs (add k8s → switch default → remove Docker) for rollback safety, or a single big-bang PR as implied by Option A?
open_decisions_blocking_implementation.recommendation: Stacked PRs. The risk of a single PR with 4,000+ lines of infrastructure changes is too high. Even within Option A (full cutover), the implementation can be phased across PRs.
open_decisions_blocking_implementation.impact_if_deferred: If deferred and a single PR is used, any issues post-merge require full revert of all changes.

open_decisions_blocking_implementation.question: What replaces IP-based session binding for defense-in-depth authentication?
open_decisions_blocking_implementation.recommendation: Kubernetes pod UID binding via downward API + short-lived rotating tokens stored in k8s Secrets.
open_decisions_blocking_implementation.impact_if_deferred: If deferred, the initial k8s deployment will have weaker auth than the Docker version. Acceptable for local-only k3s, but must be resolved before any multi-tenant deployment.

open_decisions_blocking_implementation.question: For the initial k3s deployment, is hostPath sufficient for worktree sharing, or should NFS/Longhorn be set up from the start?
open_decisions_blocking_implementation.recommendation: hostPath for initial k3s (single-node). Define a StorageBackend interface to swap later. This matches current Docker behavior most closely.
open_decisions_blocking_implementation.impact_if_deferred: N/A — this decision is needed before implementation begins.

recommendations: Phase the implementation via stacked PRs even within Option A's full-cutover scope — this provides rollback points without maintaining dual backends
Prioritize NetworkPolicy implementation and testing above all other work — this is the security-critical path
Resolve the 6 open decisions from the analysis (ContainerBackend type, storage approach, Dockerfiles, GHCR, .git shadow, integration tests) before implementation begins
Create a test coverage mapping document before rewriting integration tests
Tag the last Docker-based commit for emergency rollback
Run k3s + Calico setup on all team members' machines to validate developer experience before merging
